#2690. Bayern Munich News: Did Uli Hoeneß have good intentions with Jamal Musiala comments?; €300 million for Michael Olise?; and MORE!

Bayern Munich legend Uli Hoeneß has been on a bit of a warpath of late.

The honorary president has been critical of Bayern Munich youngsters Jamal Musiala and Lennart Karl, but has not crossed the line into creating a headache—at least not yet. While many are unhappy with the comments from Hoeneß, Sport Bild journalist Christian Falk thinks that the remarks were not coming from a place of malice:

So, Uli Hoeneß decided to open up the topic of Musiala's salary, pointing to the fact that the German international is one of the best earners at the club, and they're not sure if he'll ever be back to his best again, back when he first signed the deal, due to his health concerns. This is a really difficult topic. Not everyone is fine with the fact that Hoeneß raised the topic – and believe me, the Musiala side is not fine with it either! Also, Vincent Kompany said that before the injury, he saw the best Jamal Musiala in training since he joined the club from Burnley. So, no one can say if the medicine will have any impact on his performance levels on the pitch. At the moment, he's on the road to recovery. He's got a break away from Jürgen Klopp's Germany side, so he can enjoy more sessions in Munich.

He is one of the top earners at FC Bayern. Harry Kane obviously leapfrogged him with his new contract. It's a lot of money in Germany. Everyone is aware of this and is aware of the fact that performances have to match the salary. But it's still a difficult thing to talk about. Both sides agreed to the contract at the time. Uli Hoeneß had the idea that if one can't perform like they used to, perhaps there should be a sign made to the club from the player that they could give up some portion of their salary. No one has ever done this before and I don't think it will happen. Ultimately, I don't think any of this helps Jamal Musiala while he's recovering.

But you have to remember that it's not coming from a bad place with Uli Hoeneß. For the Bayern chief, the club is the most important thing. Therefore, he's playing the bad guy. He knows not everyone will be keen to cheer on his suggestions, but he wants the best for FC Bayern. He's the godfather of Bayern Munich, and perhaps the only person who's allowed to raise a point like this.

Hoeneß has earned the right to say a lot… no doubt. Some of today's athletes, however, are not exactly the most hardened for public criticism. Hopefully, these recent incidents will just be a blip on the radar for the players as the club seeks to get the most out of each youngster.

#2689. Week 10 Stock Up, Stock Down: Mayeday

Week 10 was one where the lows felt higher than the highs. Drake Maye went down and took the whole Patriots offense with him. Carson Beck started his first game and the impact may have cratered the entire Arizona offense going forward, and Jonathan Taylor just might not escape generic RB1 hell. Let's discuss.

Tyson followed up a 4/30 debut with a triumph of modern target volume, managing 11/80 on 3 targets as no Saints player other than him managed more than five.

The 80 is the key here – I don't think that Tyson needs to go skyrocketing up into the WR2 range based on this. The Saints just aren't playing like that kind of offense right now. But I do think it at least inches into the realm of possibility down the stretch.

We all knew that first-round pick Tyson would get a chance to do this sort of thing, and though the Saints didn't win this game, they did establish that they're willing to use him quite a bit. I'm not quite buying the idea that he is now the offense's No. 1 option and that all Chris Olave shares are headed to the dumpster, but I do think he's going to crowd out some of the other ancillary targets in this offense.

I take no pleasure in noting that RB2 was already down bad enough with four teams on bye to have time-share backs as easy No. 2 runners. The Texans lost Woody Marks to a concussion halfway through Sunday's disastrous loss to the Browns and will now be in line to be Houston's No. 1 back on Thursday night assuming David Montgomery can't get off the mat.

I'm going to level with you here: I don't think Demercado is good. I also don't think the Texans can run the ball well. But this remains to some extent a volume game, and Demercado could be the No. 1 back against a Colts defense that has been dastardly for most of the season. He's not someone to blow the whole FAAB wad on, but Demercado could give you a big game on Thursday before fading back into anonymity.

The Tennessee Titans offense has been … cooking(?) since the bye. They've now scored at least 20 points in each of their last four games, and they're playing the Cowboys next week. I already know that you don't believe me that this is happening, and I understand and accept that. You can skip on to the next capsule to read about someone who matters.

Well, you're still here for some reason. Ayomanor has played at least 50 snaps in each of the last three games, he's found 22 targets over those three games and turned in his first useful box score of the season with 79 scoreless yards against the Jaguars. At the same time, the Titans defense has absolutely collapsed, allowing 40 to the Bengals and Jaguars after the Jeffrey Simmons and Amani Hooker trades.

This team has become a points funnel all of the sudden. And, again, they're playing the Cowboys next week. I'm not telling you Ayomanor is a superstar waiting to be born. But there are six teams on bye next week, and you're going to need to make some weird roster decisions. Ayomanor might just be a good enough WR3 to get you through something next week against Dallas' barely-there defense.

Kansas City's hilarious beatdown of the Falcons culminated in Downs notching 4/53/1, the touchdown being just his second of the season. However, the additional funny context here is that Downs played just 10 offensive snaps in his first game as a Chief.

We've been burned by Downs before, of course, but with Eternal Non-Entity Xavier Worthy in front of him, it's easy to understand that Downs is going to eventually feast on a larger play volume. Is it going to be a Rashee Rice volume? That I'm not yet sure of. But I am pretty sure that Downs is going to do well enough that fantasy managers will be happy.

Going forward, it's going to feel easy to pencil Downs in as a WR3. There's also going to be plenty of runway to grow. The Colts part of his season never happened. Please stop asking about it.

(If you're looking for Emmett Johnson praise, you're late, I did that after Week 8.)

Drake Maye went down with an ankle injury early in the first quarter, effectively sabotaging the offense. A.J. Brown left with his own injury near the end of the game. Neither player returned, and Patriots coach Mike Vrabel deferred to testing. The early news on Maye from PFT was not exactly encouraging.

New England is on bye, of course, which helps the odds that Maye won't miss much time. But if he does miss time – and we've seen enough hints that this might happen – this offense looked dead in the water with Tommy DeVito under center. Unfortunately, when you write this column, you understand that this kind of death comes for a fantasy offense a few times a year.

It would be irresponsible to pretend that we know what kind of absence Maye's looking at, but even if it's not a multi-week one, you can't be starting Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner with DeVito under center. That's just not viable, as we saw today. Tertiary receivers without Brown's health will be tough plays. It's a top-to-bottom tough scene.

Congratulations to Alvin Kamara on his two touchdowns. He saw just 16 snaps in a messy situation and will be hard to trust as a FLEX play going forward. Travis Etienne didn't exactly establish himself as the lead back, but he did muddy up Kamara's receiving situation enough to make Kamara himself only a touchdown-or-bust play.

As for Johnson, in his last four games he has not crossed four targets and has just one pity touchdown to show for a grand total of 69 yards of work over that time frame. This offense is running out of effectiveness and volume to get tertiary targets involved. Perhaps Jordyn Tyson's emergence will cause teams to play them differently, but I don't see how you could pretend to be happy starting Johnson given how his last month of returns have gone. I'd classify Johnson as a TE2 at this point.

Nobody is saying that McBride is unplayable in fantasy football or anything like that, but what we are now dealing with is rookie Carson Beck, and I think there's a reasonable case to make that McBride's overall TE1 ceiling is impacted by this.

To be clear: I wouldn't put an enormous amount of stock in this rogue 5/37 line. The Rams are a great defense, and Myles Garrett is finally healthy. The Cardinals only managed to possess the ball for 17:37 of the 60 minutes of football, which I'm told is very bad.

But given the lack of receiving talent around him and a rookie quarterback who took five sacks and was picked off twice in his first start, I think we at least need to shift the window a bit on what we think will happen going forward. I would expect more 7/85s than 11/135s over the rest of the season with the quarterback and receiver downgrades.

The less I can say about the rest of this receiving corps, the better. Only one other receiver caught more than one ball.

With the Colts really and truly playing out the string here, is there really a reason for them to push Taylor? They seem very content to roll out Seth McGowan for 20 snaps a game and McGowan, to his credit, has taken advantage of the opportunities. He's averaging 4.8 yards per carry on the season and has vultured a score from Taylor in each of the last two weeks. He's not exactly decimating Taylor's workload, but McGowan is doing just enough to make RB1 upside a fading dream for the established vet.

I think Taylor is a great player, but other than the fact that he's going to destroy the Texans on Thursday Night because they have not gotten straight with whatever deity they pray to, why would they push a guy who they might have the next general manager move next offseason? To what end? If they weren't going to pedal Taylor to the floor against the Dolphins to get a win, there's no reason to believe that'll happen the rest of the season.

Will he be a reasonable RB1? Of course he will. But the guy who might threaten the overall RB1 ranks? He might have had his last hurrah against the Falcons in Europe roughly a year ago. This is just a steady contributor profile, no more, no less.

#2688. NBA News: Jaylen Clark out 2 weeks

After an abysmal performance against a basement-dwelling Chicago Bulls team on Saturday night, things got worse the next day. The Minnesota Timberwolves officially announced that Jaylen Clark, our favorite try-hard defensive stopper, would miss the next two weeks at minimum with a right hamstring strain.

Here's the play where Clark got injured early in the second quarter, making a hustle play and diving into the Minnesota bench.

This is certainly something that will be a significant blow to the Wolves. Though Clark averages just over 13 minutes per game, he is fourth on the team in defensive rating (100.3). He's been one of, if not the best, on-ball defender for Minnesota. He constantly injects energy into his team when they need it most. Jaylen has also been a 36% three-point shooter so far this season, acting as a valuable release valve on the perimeter.

"Clark County" will miss at least the next eight games in the next 14 days before he's reevaluated. Soft tissue injuries are notoriously easy to reaggravate, thus it's safe to expect he will miss well over double-digit games. When you consider Jaylen's style of play – lots of quick burst lateral movement – he could be on the shelf for at least a month next to Anthony Edwards and Donte DiVincenzo.

So who will step up in the rotation from the depth chart?

I have long since been a fan of two-way guard Zyon Pullin, but he is certainly an offense-oriented player who doesn't really provide what Clark does. Rookie Isaiah Evans is earning his stripes in the G League and likely one of the less effective defensive players on the roster. I could easily see Finch divvying Jaylen's minutes over to currently involved players like Bones Hyland and Terrence Shannon Jr.

But can I make a quick case for "no longer the worst player in the NBA," Cody Williams?

The younger Williams brother has appeared in just seven of 13 games for the Wolves this season, all in "development time." However, he did show multiple flashes of his potential during the preseason. Cody impressed in a spot preseason start against the reigning champion New York Knicks, locking up 2026 Finals MVP Jalen Brunson.

Zach Lowe had a lot of positive things to say about Williams, including his defensive improvement, at the end of last season. I'm not calling for Williams to soak up Clark's entire 13 minute role, but he fits what Minnesota is losing in Clark the most. Here's a list of guards the Wolves will face in the next two to three weeks:

There will certainly be times where LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels, Ayo Dosunmu, or Bones Hyland either falls into foul trouble or just need relief guarding those difficult assignments. When that happens, the need to get an active body who is athletic and long will be especially important.

This is the opportunity that many players in Cody's shoes hope for. He's still just 20 years old (soon to be 21 this week), but has years of experience under his belt for a tanking team. Minnesota will need his services out of desperation and he can shed that early career label as a draft bust. It's the perfect storm of supply meeting demand.

Williams also wears jersey number 9 which, as we all know, is a magical number.

If it were up to you, who would you most like to see replace Clark's minutes? Are you on the Cody Caboose like me? Or do you prefer another option? What is Ricky Rubio up to these days?

#2684. Dak Prescott: 49ers fans "were more present than ours"

On Sunday, America’s Team wasn’t even Dallas’s Team. 49ers fans showed up in big numbers for the game against the Cowboys at AT&T Stadium.

After the game, Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott was asked whether the home team had to use the silent count.

“No, we didn’t go on the silent count,” Prescott said. "[We] anticipated it. I think y’all even potentially asked me on Thursday about it, having this many 49er fans there. Tricked myself and told myself early on that the red was for my high school.

Still, it’s always a bad look when too many fans of the opposing team show up for a road game. On Sunday, 49ers fans found their way to buy tickets and infiltrate the venue.

And their fans got to see the Niners move to 8-1 on the season.

#2682. San Antonio vs. Utah, Final Score: Harper leads Spurs’ final push past Jazz, 110-102

Ascending star Dylan Harper scored 16 of his team's last 24 points to help San Antonio (12-2) claim its 12th straight victory and third straight this season over the Jazz. With the game still very much in doubt, Victor Wembanyama hit a fadeaway jumper and blocked a Keyonte George floater, and Keldon Johnson saved the ensuing carom from falling out of bounds and chased down an offensive rebound at the other end and scored a putback to put the Spurs up four in the penultimate seconds.

In a game with an exasperating amount of runs that were often one after another, Utah staged a 19-7 run spanning hte third and fourth quarters to erase the Spurs' biggest lead of the night (9) and get into the driver's seat until the visitors made that final 24-13 push.

Harper (31 points, 9 assists, and 4 assists) single-handedly willed San Antonio to victory with audacious and self-assured shotmaking throughout those critical fourth quarter minutes. Wembanyama (23 points, 9 rebounds, 5 assists, and 4 blocks) carried the offenisve production throughout the first three quarters. Stephon Castle (20 points, 9 assists, and 4 steals) and reserve Jordan McLaughlin (10 points) assured Fox wouldn't be missed TOO much. Johnson (11 points and 10 rebounds) was a menacing presence for the Spurs in the second half and especially in the waning moments.

Mo Bamba (26 points [6-for-6 from three], 5 rebounds, and 4 assists) performed admirably again in the absence of the star-studded Jazz starting bigs. Backup Brice Sensabaugh (14 points and 7 rebounds) and rookie Darryn Peterson (17 points, 5 rebounds, and 4 assists) led a group of contributors that supplied plentiful support for Bamba and made up for an off-night for Keyonte George (13 points, 8 assists, and 4 rebounds).

The teams mirrored each other over the opening minutes – with Wembanyama and Bamba taking center stage before Rutgers' Harper and Bailey exchanged buckets. While the bigs' turned away several shots at or near the rim, the Jazz swingmen made a flurry of threes to get themselves out front. Despite those outside bursts, the Spurs stayed neck-and-neck with their counterparts. While the hosts shot an astounding 7-for-10 fron behind the line, they still only went to the second up two, after McLaughlin kickstarted a closing 8-0 run to end the first quarter.

Bamba's third and fourth threes (without a miss) created some space between his team and San Antonio. While the teams continued to shoot well from the field, Utah's proficiency from distance made up the bulk of their advantage. After opposing 9-0 runs, the Jazz took advantage of San Antonio's errant shooting to leap back into the lead. Utah's perimeter men seemed to make quite a few shots late in the clock. Wembanyama rescued a handful of possessions with his shooting and playmaking and the Spurs went to halftime slightly up 58-55.

Coming out of the break, Castle figured in one each of the Spurs' first four scores – two field goals, two freebies, and one assist. Rookie Peterson dazzled with his ability to score from different spots on the floor. Bamba and Bradley resembled Utah legend Thurl Bailey by knocking down shot after shot. A 10-0 run by San Antonio got them to 79-70. Bamba's fifth straight three without a miss tied things right back at 79. San Antonio nearly went the rest of the quarter without scoring again and the teams were deadlocked at 81 going to the final 12 minutes.

Game Clinching Play #1: Everything Harper died from the 8:07 mark of the fourth quarter to the final buzzer.

Game Clinching Play #2: With a four-point lead, Castle received a 'thank you very much' steal and threw down an uncontested windmill jam

I might be repeating myself, but Bamba continues to look like a very competent veteran out there filling in for Markkanen and Jackson, Jr.

The mountain outline on the court is immaculate despite all of the trauma those 90s Jazz teams caused us Spurs fans.

Small sample size of Fox's steady consistency… six first half turnovers in his absence.

The in-arena cams during the first timeout showcased a dance contest, and well, I won't get back those two minutes ever again.

On the Jazz broadcast, they brought in former slam dunk champion Jeremy Evans for a lengthy first half interview. #obscure2010splayers

Area 51 Sequence of the Game: Though the two hadn't found each other over many of the first 23 minutes, Castle fed Wembanyama in transition in the final minute of the half to close out the scoring.

#2680. Christian McCaffrey on career-high receiving yards: You just catch it and run as fast as you can

The 49ers running back had never had more than 121 receiving yards in a single game. He had 161 receiving yards on four catches Sunday against the Cowboys, scoring on catch-and-runs of 74 and 66 in the 49ers’ 46-40 win.

“You never know,” McCaffrey said. “You go into each game. You don’t really predict anything. Again, you just have to have the right mindset on a play that’s going to break. You trust your instincts and play fast.”

His first receiving touchdown came when Brock Purdy rolled to his right to buy time and found McCaffrey running free on the scramble drill.

“It really is backyard football at that point,” McCaffrey said. “We all played it as kids at recess, and you draw up plays on your hand, and it never happens. You ever tell a 5-year-old to run a post route, and he just runs a corner and something else, but he’s open? That’s kind of what that was. Again, I think those little decisions that you make in games, from Brock to scramble, not to just surrender the play but to keep it alive. That’s a big deal. There’s no planning that goes into that. It’s just him doing a great job playing ball.”

What turned out to be the game-winning touchdown came with 3:23 remaining when Purdy found McCaffrey, who was matched up against Von Miller, over the middle.

“They brought pressure,” McCaffrey said. “They dropped a D-end on me, so that’s a perfect look for that play. Again, it was a great job by Brock getting the ball where it needed to be. It made it easy for me.

“You just catch it and run as fast as you can to try to score. Don’t overthink it. You hope that nobody catches you, and you hope that you’re really fast so your teammates don’t catch up to you to celebrate, because it makes you look slow. We’ll have to check the tape.”

McCaffrey had a 16-yard touchdown run and 62 yards rushing. He is the first player in the Super Bowl era with at least 150 receiving yards, two receiving touchdowns, 50-plus rushing yards and at least one rushing touchdown.

#2679. Christian McCaffrey, 49ers run past Cowboys 46-40

49ers fans took over AT&T Stadium on Sunday, out-drawing and out-yelling Cowboys fans. They booed the Cowboys running onto their own field, and they loudly celebrated a 46-40 San Francisco win.

In an entertaining game, the 49ers moved to 8-1, and the Cowboys fell to 4-6.

Christian McCaffrey had a career-high 161 receiving yards on four catches, two of them touchdowns, and ran for 62 yards and a touchdown on 13 carries. He is the first player in the Super Bowl era with at least 150 receiving yards, two receiving touchdowns, 50-plus rushing yards and at least one rushing touchdown.

The 49ers led 38-19 with 11:26 remaining in the fourth quarter. But George Pickens caught a 5-yard touchdown pass, which was followed by a missed 2-point conversion. Ryan Flournoy’s 11-yard score with 3:42 left cut the Cowboys’ deficit to 38-32. The 49ers burned only 2:26 on their possession in between, punting after four plays.

The 49ers showed the Cowboys who they are, though, when Brock Purdy hit McCaffrey across the middle of the field. Von Miller, who was covering McCaffrey, and his teammates had no chance of catching the running back, who went 66 yards to the end zone.

The Cowboys didn’t go away quietly, scoring once more on CeeDee Lamb’s 1-yard reception. Dak Prescott ran in the 2-point conversion.

Dallas tried an onside kick despite having three timeouts and did not convert.

Kaelon Black, who had 11 carries for 53 yards and a touchdown, fumbled on the second-down play. Quinnen Williams forced it, but Black was able to get back on the ball. The 49ers punted, and the Cowboys were left with only 9 seconds and in need of 91 yards and a miracle.

McCaffrey’s other touchdowns were a 74-yard reception and a 16-yard run.

The 49ers had 584 yards, the third-most the Cowboys have allowed in their history. It was not far from the 49ers’ team record of 621.

Purdy set a career-high with 389 passing yards and threw three touchdowns, completing 22 of 28 passes.

George Kittle had six catches for 74 yards, and new addition Keenan Allen five for 61. Deebo Samuel had three catches for 31 yards and a touchdown and three carries for 78 yards and a touchdown.

The Cowboys couldn’t keep up, even with 439 yards.

Prescott was 30-of-51 for 343 yards with five touchdowns and an interception. Pickens had 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns, and Lamb seven for 72 yards and a touchdown. Flournoy added six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown.

#2677. Luka Dončić scores 43, leading Lakers over Suns for eighth consecutive win, tying for NBA's top record

Luka Dončić continued his scorching start to the 2026-27 NBA season, topping the 40-point mark for the seventh time in 12 games in the Los Angeles Lakers' 131-123 win over the Phoenix Suns on Sunday. He currently leads the NBA in scoring at 38.6 points per game.

Dončić scored 20 of his 43 points in the first quarter, hitting three 3-pointers as he shot 5-for-10 and the Lakers took a 33-24 lead. That advantage increased to 54-37 with five minutes to go before halftime on a Jake LaRavia 3. Yet the Suns closed out the second quarter on a 12-3 run to trim the Lakers' lead to 61-54.

In the third quarter, the Lakers started hot from behind the arc, hitting three 3-pointers (two by Quentin Grimes) as part of a 13-3 run and boosted their lead to 20 points. Eventually, that margin became 31 points with under two minutes remaining in the quarter. Dončić added 12 points to put him at 37 points going into the final 12 minutes.

Phoenix recovered to give the Lakers a game in the fourth quarter, hitting four 3-point attempts to begin the frame. A Walker Kessler tip-in dunk restored the Lakers' advantage to 113-92 with just under nine minutes remaining.

However, the Suns responded with a 15-1 surge, fueled by six points from rookie Koa Peat. A 3 from Ryan Dunn cut the Lakers' lead to 117-111 at the 4:40 mark. Collin Gillespie drove to the basket for a layup that pulled Phoenix to within five points with 1:05 left in regulation.

But another 3 from Grimes effectively put the game away for the Lakers and Dončić closed out the scoring with two free throws. However, he told sideline reporter Roqui Theus afterward that the plan was for him to sit out the fourth quarter until the Suns made the game close.

"I wasn't planning on playing the fourth quarter," Dončić said. "We gotta get better at that. … Once we get up, we gotta stay there."

The Lakers played without Austin Reaves, who missed the game due to a bone bruise in his left heel.

Overall, Dončić shot 13-of-28 from the floor, while making 12-of-14 free throws. He also notched nine assists in his 43 minutes of play. Grimes followed with 22 points, shooting 5-for-6 on 3-pointers, with 6 assists and 2 steals. Collin Sexton contributed 16 points off the bench and Kessler added 14 points with 12 rebounds.

For the Suns, Gillespie finished with 26 points (shooting 5-for-10 on 3s), 4 assists and 4 rebounds. Luke Kennard added 18 as the Suns got 78 points from their reserves. Devin Booker led the Phoenix starters with 17 points and 7 assists.

The Lakers have won eight consecutive games and improved their record to 12-2, tying the San Antonio Spurs for the NBA's best record. (The Spurs defeated the Utah Jazz on Sunday, 110-102.) Their next game is Tuesday versus the Charlotte Hornets (4-9).

#2672. Game Recap: Furious comeback by Suns bench falls short in 131-123 loss

The Lakers came out of the gates hot, and the Suns did not. From there, every time the Suns started to put together a run, the Lakers answered with a bigger run. And while the bench gave the Suns some hope with a furious comeback attempt in the fourth quarter, the Suns dug themselves far too big a hole to climb out of, ultimately falling to the Lakers at home, 131-123.

If the Suns had any hope of an upset, they needed to slow down the Lakers' potent offense, and they failed to do that for much of the afternoon. The Lakers came out of the gates hot and did not really slow down. Luka scored 20 in the first quarter on the way to a 43-point afternoon (together with nine assists), but the Suns' inability to stop Lakers not named Luka, inability to keep the Lakers off the offensive boards, and inability to stop the three is what ultimately did the team in.

Quentin Grimes scored 22 points for the Lakers, including 11 in the third quarter, while shooting 5-of-6 from three. The Lakers grabbed 12 offensive rebounds – with Walker Kessler having six of them – which led to 21 second-chance points. And the Lakers shot 16-of-41 (39%) from three, with Luka and Grimes combining to hit 10 of them.

For the Suns, the story was the fact that the starters dug such a deep hole that the bench could not get them out. Devin Booker was 4-14, Jalen Green was 4-11, and Dillon Brooks was 0-of-2 (what?!). The Suns actually out-rebounded the Lakers (42 to 40) and grabbed more offensive rebounds than the Lakers (14 to 12), but not thanks to the starters. The bench grabbed 29 of the Suns' 42 rebounds and 12 of their 14 offensive rebounds. But the Suns' bench not only outperformed the starters on the boards, but they also outperformed them overall.

Collin Gillespie led the Suns in scoring with 26 points (including 5-of-10 from three). Jordan Goodwin led the team in rebounds, with seven. Ryan Dunn grabbed four offensive rebounds, and Luke Kennard chipped in another three.

And let's not forget Koa Peat. Mr. Arizona sparked a furious fourth-quarter rally that saw the Suns' bench cut a 24-point Lakers lead to just five, before running out of steam down the stretch.

Overall, this game ended up being much closer than it felt throughout the afternoon. The Suns started the fourth quarter down by 24, and the bench was entirely responsible for the team nearly pulling this one out. Notably, Jordan Ott stuck with the bench throughout that quarter. He did not go back to the starters. It felt like the right move, but also truly confirms the lack of cohesiveness with the starting five.

At the end of the day, the Suns miss out on a chance to get to .500, falling to 5-7, as the Lakers win their eighth in a row to move to 12-2.

The Suns got off to the slowest start we've seen since opening night, letting the Lakers score the first 10 points of the game — eight of them by Luka — before Miles Bridges scored the team's first points with 9:24 left in the first quarter. The Lakers followed that 10-2 start by going on a 13-3 run, which left the Suns trailing by 18 after just over 5 minutes of playing time.

Jordan Ott went to the bench, and the bench and Devin Booker managed to trim that lead to 9 by the end of the quarter. A Booker jumper, a Collin Gillespie three, then a Kahman Maluach layup on a nice feed from Book sparked a 7-0 run, to make it a 23-12 game. From there, Book and Maluach were responsible for the rest of the Suns' points that quarter – with Book scoring eight and Man Man chipping in four.

Maluach flashed some of his defensive potential on a play where he challenged and altered a layup attempt by Sandro Mamukelashvili and showed a quick second jump by immediately blocking a Jarred Vanderbilt layup attempt.

At the end of the first, the Suns found themselves down 33-24.

With Luka out to start the second, the Suns needed to take advantage of the non-Luka minutes – and, at first, it looked like they did. The Suns started the quarter with a Gillespie three to cut the lead to six, but that was the closest they would get (until the fourth). The Suns ended up losing the non-Luka minutes – letting Collin Sexton score eight points in the second. By the time Luka came back in the game with 4:56 left in the half, the Suns found themselves down 17.

That lead ballooned to 19, before the Suns started chipping away again. At the 3:36 mark, they were down 19. At that time, the story of the game was the difference from three (with the Lakers being +12) and from the free-throw line (+7). The Lakers also grabbed seven offensive rebounds in the second frame alone.

The only player showing any true effort on the boards for the Suns at this juncture was Jordan Goodwin — who was fouled on two separate occasions while trying to grab offensive rebounds off missed free throws.

Despite only having 10 points from Booker in the first half, the Suns were only down 10 at halftime.

The third quarter started a lot like the first. The Lakers were scoring and we could not. After the Lakers scored the first eight points, the Suns finally got some points from Devin Booker with 9:28 left. But it continued to be all Lakers from there.

Just like Collin Sexton stepped up for the Lakers in the second quarter, the third quarter belonged to Quentin Grimes. Grimes, who came in shooting 28% from three on the season, scored 11 in the quarter, including three 3-pointers. Luka also scored in double figures in the third quarter, chipping in 12.

In the third, the Suns shot 9-of-21 overall and 2-of-11 from three, while the Lakers shot 14-of-23 overall and 5-of-9 from three.

The fourth quarter started with little hope and a 24-point deficit. The Suns came out and promptly scored the first six points, and after the Lakers got the lead back to 22, Collin Gillespie hit back-to-back threes to cut the lead to 16 with 10 minutes left.

But then the offensive rebounds started coming back. Thybulle had a tip-in off a missed three, then on the next possession, Kessler had a put-back dunk on a missed layup by Thybulle. The Suns were down 19 with 8:15 left, and Koa Peat checked in – making it look like Jordan Ott had decided to pack it in.

But Peat checking in resulted in a furious comeback attempt that made a mundane afternoon into an exciting one.

Peat immediately impacted the game, fighting off Kessler on a Suns miss, which allowed the team to keep possession, then scoring on a strong shot over Kessler.

Collin Gillespie was also not ready for the game to be called, as he drew an and-1 on the next possession, to get the Suns within 14. This brought Luka and his 37 points back into the game. The first possession of Luka's return resulted in a turnover, and Gillespie missed a step-through jumper, but Peat was there for the tip-in. Suns down 12 with just over six minutes to go.

The Suns used a 10-1 run to find themselves down single digits with 5:02 to go. And they kept chipping away.

A Ryan Dunn three cut the lead to six with 4:37 left. Jake Laravia answers with a three of his own, but then Luke Kennard drops one to make it a six-point game again, but a missed three by Laravia followed by an offensive rebound and then a BANKED in three by Lavaria sealed the game for the Lakers.

An exciting comeback, but, ultimately, a 131-123 loss — and a loss that just further magnifies the obvious disconnect amongst the Suns starters. But still, Koa Peat…

The Suns hit the road immediately for an away matchup tomorrow against the Denver Nuggets.

#2670. Germany dominate Serbia in rain-soaked Nations League clash

Germany have made a good start to the last Nations League phase in 2026, beating Serbia 3-1 in a rain-soaked contest. Goals from Wirtz and debutant Gruda mean that Germany still have the chance to top their Nations League group.

The unusual behind-closed-doors atmosphere has seen selected groups of children under 15 admitted alongside teachers and football coaches following UEFA sanctions against Serbia for discrimination. However, the game still delivered on the entertainment front.

Jürgen Klopp's side needed just two minutes to break the deadlock, with Kai Havertz getting on the end of a corner before his attempt was deflected into the net by Srdan Babić for an own goal.

Germany doubled their advantage in the 14th minute following a brilliant, Klopp-esque pressing sequence. Aleksandar Pavlović played a superb through ball to Havertz, whose effort was denied by goalkeeper Vanja Milinković-Savić. Florian Wirtz reacted quickest to the rebound and calmly chipped the ball into the net.

Germany dominated the remainder of the first half, enjoying 75% possession and completing 94% of their passes. Their superiority continued after the break, with Brajan Gruda capping a fantastic solo run with a clinical finish in the 50th minute to make it 3-0.

Serbia responded just six minutes later. Babić made amends for his earlier own goal by reacting quickest after Stefan Gudelj's header from a free kick was saved, converting the rebound to give the hosts a lifeline.

Joshua Kimmich thought he had restored Germany's three-goal advantage shortly afterwards with a powerful low strike from the edge of the box. However, the goal was correctly ruled out due to Kai Havertz's passive offside position.

Derry Scherhant, one of Germany's standout performers under Klopp so far, had enjoyed a relatively quiet evening but came close to scoring in the 70th minute. After cutting inside from the left, his effort beat the goalkeeper but struck the woodwork.

Serbia substitute Aleksandar Mitrović also came close to scoring, but Marc-André ter Stegen stood firm to keep his effort out. Things then went from bad to worse for the hosts as Vanja Dragojevic received a straight red card for a dangerous challenge on Germany captain Joshua Kimmich, accidentally standing on his ankle.

Dragojević was not the only Serbian to leave the pitch early. Substitute Andrija Zivković also saw red after picking up two yellow cards in quick succession following an animated exchange with the referee shortly before full-time.

Klopp used the opportunity to introduce several other Bundesliga names, including Niclas Füllkrug, Felix Nmecha and Said El Mala. However, none managed to make a significant impact during their limited time on the pitch. They could get another opportunity when Germany face the Netherlands on Monday.

The match also marked a historic first for Germany, with Kimmich and Pavlović starting together as a double pivot for the first time. The partnership showed plenty of promise and could become a regular feature under Klopp.

Finally, it was also Germany's last appearance in their long-standing partnership with Adidas. Given the convincing performance, it was certainly a fitting farewell.

PHOENIX (AP) — Luka Doncic scored 43 points and Los Angeles stretched their winning streak to eight games by holding off Phoenix.

It did little to slow down the NBA's top scoring team — through three quarters.

Quentin Grimes banked in a 3-pointer with 34 seconds left and Doncic sealed it with two free throws.

Doncic, the NBA's leading scorer, hit five 3-pointers and went 12 for 14 on free throws for his sixth 40-point game this season. Grimes went 5 of 6 from 3 to finish with 22 points.

TORONTO (AP) — Jalen Brunson made a tiebreaking 3-pointer with 33 seconds remaining in overtime and New York beat Toronto, their 14th straight win over the Raptors.

Brunson scored 28 points, and Karl-Anthony Towns had 28 points and 17 rebounds for the Knicks, who trailed by 13 points in the fourth quarter.

Landry Shamet scored 23 points and OG Anunoby had 21 against his former team as the defending NBA champions snapped a two-game losing streak.

Scottie Barnes scored 30 points and Jamal Shead added 19 but the Raptors lost their fourth straight and seventh in nine.

Toronto has led by double digits in each of its past three defeats. The Raptors couldn't hold a 22-point lead against Boston on Wednesday, and blew a 17-point edge at Philadelphia on Thursday.

Boston pulled its starters after that but still pulled ahead by 41 in the final quarter.

Castle's steal and dunk with 47.2 seconds remaining capped a 14-4 run and extended San Antonio's lead to 108-102.

Milwaukee built a 22-point lead early in the second quarter before Atlanta stormed back to take a 55-53 lead at the half on Dyson Daniels' layup just ahead of the horn.

#2666. 3 bleak thoughts after the Mavericks’ no-show in 131-94 loss at the Boston Celtics

The last three games make it clear. This season is all about managing expectations for fans of the Dallas Mavericks (7-7). But good grief.

The Mavericks dropped the second game of a back-to-back set in horrifying fashion, 131-94, in a Sunday matinee against the Boston Celtics (11-2) at TD Garden.

The unbridled optimism that came along with a surprise 7-4 start has been tempered, to say the least, after a pair of stinkers at the Minnesota Timberwolves and the Cleveland Cavaliers, followed by Sunday's scheduled loss, when the Mavs were again without star 34-year-old guard Kyrie Irving, due to injury management (rest).

The Celtics poured in three of their first four 3-point attempts to jump out to an 11-2 lead three minutes into the game, and the tone was set quickly. The Mavs didn't make their first shot from the field until Zaccharie Risacher hit a long jumper from the corner with 5:22 left in the first. The starting lineup of Cooper Flagg, Caleb Martin, Naji Marshall, Daniel Gafford and PJ Washington provided zero floor spacing on the offensive end.

And so, naturally, the Celtics' early lead swelled to 19-4 after Jordan Walsh went to the basket for six straight points on three straight possessions less than five minutes into the game. If Cooper Flagg isn't going out of his mind on offense, the roster as constructed for Sunday's game just doesn't stand a chance against the league's best teams.

Boston canned seven triples in the first quarter, while the Mavs shot an abysmal 2-of-18 from the field. The game was basically over as the Celtics led by an appalling 42-9 count after one. It goes without saying that the nine points were the lowest scoring output for the Mavs of the young 2026-27 season, but what was worse is that the team appeared to let it affect their effort on defense, as well.

The Mavericks woke up a little in the second quarter, but waking up after you're down 35 points is not worth a whole hell of a lot. A little 9-0 run late in the frame pulled the Mavs to within 59-34, but it seems laughable to even mention developments like that in the course of such a monumental shellacking.

Dallas turned the ball over 12 times in the first half to offset the team's five second-quarter 3-point makes, and Boston carried a lopsided 67-37 lead into the halftime break.

Flagg's early run of brilliance to start the season has hit a hard car crash of a stop. He shot a combined 11-of-31 in the two losses leading up to Sunday's game at Boston, and he followed that up by missing all three of his first-quarter shot attempts.

We see apex Flagg, as we've learned, when he plays next to competent guards, and that was simply not the case against the Celtics. The starting lineup at Boston featured exactly zero guards, and when Walter Clayton Jr. and Marcus Sasser entered halfway into the first, they offered little to no help on either end. Clayton came back in the second and scored eight points on two made 3-pointers, but the damage had been done at that point.

The Celtics' defense concentrated all their efforts into containing Flagg, because Flagg was the only viable source of offense left on Dallas' injury-riddled roster. He finally connected on his first field goal early in the second, on the low block through the foul of Payton Pritchard. But after two more 3-balls from the Celtics on the other end, the Celtics' lead had ballooned to 50-15 with nine minutes left in the first half.

There will be angst, and a certain amount of angst is warranted here, but circumstances aren't helping the 19-year-old star, either. He scored just five points in the first half and finished with 17 on 5-of-15 shooting in the loss.

Let's just get this out of the way and move on, shall we? Jayson Tatum torched the Mavericks for 21 of his game-high 32 points in the third quarter to lead way for the Celtics in the win. Derrick White added 16. Eight different Celtics made two or more 3-pointers, including Tatum, who put in five of them.

Risacher led the Mavericks with 18 off the bench on 8-of-9 shooting.

#2664. Mitch Albom: Aidan Hutchinson injury gives Lions big lesson on celebrations

There's a common German expression: Erst wägen, dann wagen. It means weigh the risks, then act.

Or, to bring it closer to English, look before you leap.

Aidan Hutchinson should have heeded either version in Munich on Sunday, Nov. 15, after bringing down New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye on an inspiring early sack.

Instead, the Detroit Lions defensive lineman celebrated by leaping into the air like a Zulu warrior and landing hard on his right leg, which buckled at the knee and sent him to the ground like a broken marionette.

I'm sure no one feels worse than Hutchinson today, and this is not meant to rub it in. But no Lion – and no NFL player for that matter – should miss playing time due to a celebration. It's unnecessary. It's over the top. And the league is rife with examples of how this has backfired in the past:

Remember Detroit's Stephen Tulloch, who celebrated sacking Green Bay's Aaron Rodgers in September 2014 with a leap of his own, followed by a pelvic thrust – mimicking Rodgers' State Farm "Discount Double Check" – followed by an instant collapse with a torn ACL?

Remember Lamarr Houston of the Chicago Bears the next month, doing the same thing after sacking Patriots QB Jimmy Garoppolo? He tore his ACL. Missed the rest of the season.

You don't need more examples than that (although there are plenty of them, including quarterback Gus Frerotte intentionally banging his head on a concrete wall). But it's simple, folks. You want to celebrate? Stay on the ground. Don't leap. Don't twist. Act like you've been there before.

Instead, the Lions may have lost Hutchinson, their most important defensive player, just when their defense was rounding into postseason form.

There's another German expression: So ein Pech!

Remember, Hutchinson's setback comes on the heels of the Lions losing equally critical defensive star linebacker Jack Campbell, who remains out indefinitely after needing to be carted off the field two weeks ago. But Campbell was hurt on a terrible collision, the kind of football play that is tragic and unpredictable.

The good news, in both cases, is that the rest of the Detroit defense stepped up big time. The Lions allowed just 10 points and 151 yards of offense to the Pats on Sunday, while recording five sacks and an interception. Yes, this was almost all against backup quarterback Tommy DeVito, who at times played more like Danny DeVito, and rendered the Pats far less dangerous than Maye, last year's MVP runner-up.

But you face what you face, and the Lions defense did itself proud.

"This is the second time this has happened," Dan Campbell told the media after the game, referring to Campbell and Hutch's injuries, "and our guys have responded in a tough situation and didn't bat an eye. …

"We did what we had to do to get out of this game with a win."

Still, if I'm the coach, I'm quietly issuing an edict to my team: You want to celebrate? Both feet on the ground.

Or get down on all fours, which is something the Lions did after Amon-Ra St. Brown's second long touchdown of the game. Nearly the entire offense formed a caterpillar walk along the back of the end zone.

I mean, when was the last time you heard of a caterpillar tearing his ACL?

Which brings us to the happier part of Sunday's beatdown of last year's AFC Super Bowl representative: The Detroit offense.

The Lions racked up nearly 500 yards. St. Brown was his normal superstar self, and given how beloved he is in Germany (his mother was born there, he speaks fluent German and was the toast of Munich the past three days) it was fitting that he scored the game's first touchdown, a beautiful sideline pass where he lost his defender with a step back, then raced 56 yards through the entire defense, into the end zone.

His second touchdown was truly a team effort. On third-and-10 in the third quarter, Jared Goff found St. Brown cutting to the middle, hit him in stride, and St. Brown motored through the defense to within a few yards of the goal line. Then, Isaac TeSlaa began pulling him in, Sam LaPorta started pushing him from behind, and the rest of the Lions plowed alongside, until, like a snowball down the Alps, St. Brown rolled into the end zone for another TD.

"It's been one of the most fun games I've ever had," he told Fox after the win. "… I'm sad to leave."

Well, hey. If St. Brown wants to stay in Germany, then Jahmyr Gibbs might want to buy a villa on the Isar River.

Gibbs had his biggest game of the season: 153 yards rushing, 99 yards receiving (both team highs) plus two touchdowns. He was a ball of unstoppable energy, blazing through holes (thanks to a much more effective offensive line) and taking short passes and turning them into long gains.

Gibbs simply gets better and better, and, on certain Sundays, just seems unstoppable. He allows Goff the luxury of drawing defenses on play actions and opens up everything for the rest of the high-powered offense. The Lions scored 35 points Sunday and as St. Brown said, "I still feel like we left some meat on the bone."

So the Lions have now won five in a row, are tied atop the NFC North and seem a long way from the hand-wringing Hamlets they were at 2-2 with their defense in the crapper.

Had Hutchinson not literally thrown himself into a real conundrum, the Lions would be flying back from Europe as giddy as a group of college backpackers on their first overseas trip.

Instead, Detroit may be looking at missing the two biggest parts of its defense for the upcoming toughest stretch of the season.

Everyone knows Hutch didn't mean it. Everyone knows he feels awful about it. But there is simply no excuse for this ever happening to a Lion again. Please. Guys. Leave the takeoffs and landings to the team plane. Erst wägen, dann wagen. Celebrate here on earth.

Contact Mitch Albom: malbom@freepress.com. Check out the latest updates on his charities, books and events at MitchAlbom.com. Follow @mitchalbom on x.com.

This article originally appeared on Detroit Free Press: Mitch Albom: Aidan Hutchinson injury gives Lions big lesson on celebrations

#2661. Celtics throttle Mavericks, 131-94, thanks to magnificent 42-9 1st quarter

Some NBA games are won late in the fourth quarter, with dramatic twists and turns in the final seconds and elite shotmaking from the game's brightest stars.

Sunday was not one of those games. This one was over before many fans settled into their seats, as the Celtics led by 33 through 1 en route to a dominant 131-94 victory at TD Garden.

"We were playing well, forcing them into shots we want them to take, and they missed some shots," said Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla.

Boston (11-2) has now won six straight, including four by 20 or more, and is still in first place in the Eastern Conference. Dallas (7-7), playing without Kyrie Irving (knee) on the second night of a back to back, looked outmatched in every facet early.

Jayson Tatum led the way with 32 points (11-of-18 shooting), 6 rebounds and 6 assists. Boston shot 51 percent as a team, leaving no doubt and improving to 6-0 at home on the season.

The Celtics absolutely dominated the first quarter, building a 42-9 advantage through 1 with a truly spectacular performance. Yes, it was the largest lead after the first quarter in franchise history. It felt like it, too.

Boston shot 59 percent from the floor and 54 percent from 3, while Dallas was at 11 percent from the field and 0 percent from distance. The Celtics racked up 14 points in the paint, compared to 2 for the Mavericks, and won the rebounding battle, 16-10.

Boston could do no wrong. Dallas could do no right.

"We tried to shrink the floor as much as possible and cause havoc," said Celtics wing Jordan Walsh.

Walsh played with conviction and purpose and helped set the tone early, and Derrick White (16 points) found a rhythm early to help extend the lead. Seemingly every shot the Celtics threw up went in, as the action resembled a varsity team scrimmaging a junior varsity team.

The Mavericks found their footing in the second quarter and chipped away, but the Celtics preserved a 67-37 lead heading into halftime following a relatively even second quarter.

"Obviously it's easy to really bring it when it's a close game, or things like that," Tatum said. "Just trying to challenge our mindset of we're up 25 to 30, can you try to put the game away? I think we did a really good job of that today."

Tatum, Pritchard and White continued to flourish, and Sam Hauser provided strong minutes off the bench. Zaccharie Risacher (18 points) paced Dallas with 9 in the half, but Cooper Flagg (17) struggled and the Mavericks turned it over six more times in the quarter.

Eleven players saw the floor for Boston and nine scored, led by White with 11.

The Celtics kept their target practice going in the third quarter, as Paul George and Walsh hit back-to-back corner 3's to push the margin to 34. Neemias Queta added one of his own from the other corner to improve to 4 of 5 from distance on the season.

"His growth and his role has gone kind of under the radar," Mazzulla said of Queta. "He's more important than just with defense. He's important in the locker room, he's important on the offensive end. He continues to get better and better. It's easy to overlook it because of how easy he makes it."

Flagg got going in the third, but Tatum continued to cook and kept the lead hovering around 30 most of the way.

Tatum drilled a step-back 3 with 4.3 seconds left to make it 104-71 through three. He finished the quarter with 21 and continued to look like pre-injury Tatum.

The Celtics started the fourth with Baylor Scheierman, Devin Carter, Ron Harper Jr., Hugo González and Luka Garza, and they continued to play the brand of basketball that got Boston to that point.

Harper Jr. converted inside, Scheierman and Harper Jr. swished consecutive 3's and Garza delivered inside to push it to 40, 117-77, with 8:58 to go.

"The start of the fourth quarter, we made them call the first timeout," Mazzulla said.

Gino Time came with 2:51 remaining and the Celtics up 36. The win streak is alive, and the Celtics are looking very much like contenders.

#2660. Joe Burrow matches Peyton Manning's record for consecutive games with at least four TDs

Joe Burrow has accomplished something that had not been done for over 20 years.

With his 4-yard touchdown to Chase Brown in the third quarter, Burrow became the first since Peyton Manning in 2004 to have at least four total touchdowns in five consecutive games, which is the longest streak in NFL history.

Manning would win his second MVP award for his 2004 season.

Burrow has thrown for four, four, five, three, and now four in his last six games. He’s also had a rushing touchdown in each of the last two weeks before Sunday’s matchup against Pittsburgh.

#2658. Mavericks score just 9 points in opening quarter during historic loss to Jayson Tatum, Celtics

The Dallas Mavericks got out to a horrific and historically bad start on Sunday night at TD Garden.

The Boston Celtics rolled to a 42-9 lead in the opening quarter. That marked Boston's largest lead at the end of the first period in franchise history.

It gets even worse for the Mavericks. The Celtics' 42-9 scoring margin was the best from any team in the league in any quarter since 1987, when the Los Angeles Lakers outscored the Sacramento Kings 40-4 in the first quarter, according to ESPN. It was also the third-best mark by a team in a quarter in the shot-clock era, which started back in 1954.

Remarkably, it wasn't the Mavericks' worst quarter in franchise history. They managed just two points in a quarter in a game against the Los Angeles Lakers in 1997.

On Sunday, the Mavericks made just two of their first 18 field-goal attempts in the opening quarter, and went a brutal 0 of 8 from behind the arc. Of their nine points in the opening frame, five of them came from the free-throw line.

"I didn't feel like we were turning it over early," Mavericks coach Dusty May said, via the Dallas Morning News' Mike Curtis. "I felt like we had some decent looks. We didn't convert them. I'd have to go back and look at the film for any specifics of why we weren't able to score."

And while things did get better for the Mavericks, it was far too late to make a difference. The Celtics took a 30-point lead into the locker room at halftime, and then rolled to the 131-94 victory.

Jayson Tatum led Boston with 32 points, 6 rebounds and 6 assists while shooting 11 of 18 from the field in the win. Derrick White added 16 points, and Baylor Scheierman finished with 12 points and five rebounds off the bench. Boston shot 51% from the field as a team and forced 17 turnovers.

The Celtics are now 11-2 on the season. They have won six straight, too, and hold a slight lead over the Philadelphia 76ers in the Eastern Conference standings.

Zaccharie Risacher led the Mavericks with 18 points off the bench after he went 8 of 9 from the field. Cooper Flagg finished with 17 points, and Walter Clayton added 13 points. The Mavericks were coming off a loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers in Ohio on Saturday night.

They have now lost three in a row and sit at 7-7 on the season. Thankfully, after a rough three-game road trip capped by a truly bad outing on Sunday, Flagg and the Mavericks will have three days to recover. They'll host the Golden State Warriors on Wednesday night.

#2656. Sunday Night Football: Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase torch Steelers in 38-18 Bengals victory

The Bengals wanted to create a special “white out” environment for Sunday’s game, with the home team wearing its “White Bengal” uniform and helmet.

After the performance against the Steelers, they may want to make that alternate kit permanent.

Quarterback Joe Burrow and receiver Ja’Marr Chase were stellar on Sunday night, with Cincinnati defeating division-rival Pittsburgh 38-18.

In just the first half, Burrow had 302 yards and three touchdowns before finishing the contest 35-of-44 for 409 yards with four TDs. Joe Flacco came in for mop-up duty midway through the final period.

Burrow also tied Peyton Manning’s record streak of five consecutive games of at least four touchdowns.

As he often is, Chase was Burrow’s favorite target, catching 11 passes for 231 yards. While Chase didn’t have a touchdown himself, he caught deep bombs of 53 and 43 yards that helped set up scores.

It was the third-highest output of Chase’s career and the fourth time he’s gone over 200 yards in a regular-season game.

The Bengals scored on four of their five first-half possessions, and would have made it all five if Evan McPherson had hit his 43-yard field goal attempt that sailed wide right. That was McPherson’s first missed kick of the season.

But McPherson had opened the scoring with a 24-yard field goal to cap the opening drive. Drew Sample had a 3-yard TD catch, Chase Brown had a 2-yard score, and Dohnte Meyers had a 15-yard touchdown reception to give the Bengals a 24-3 halftime lead.

Brown caught his second touchdown in the third quarter to make it 31-3. And Samaje Perine closed the Bengals’ scoring with his 1-yard touchdown run with 10:08 left in the fourth quarter.

As well as Cincinnati’s offense played, the defense may have been better. Aaron Rodgers started the contest 0-of-8 passing, with his first completion not coming until there was 4:31 left in the second quarter.

Pittsburgh had just four first downs and 40 total yards at halftime.

Rodgers ended the night 15-of-29 for 143 yards with two touchdowns, both of which came in the fourth quarter after the game was out of reach. Rodgers was also sacked three times.

With the win, the Bengals are now 7-2 on the season and have sole possession of first place in the AFC North. They will have an extra day to prepare, as they’ll face the Commanders next Monday night.

The Steelers fall to 6-3 and will be on the road to face the Eagles next Sunday afternoon.

#2652. Utah Jazz lose heartbreaking game against San Antonio Spurs

The Jazz welcomed the red-hot San Antonio Spurs to the Delta Center on Sunday afternoon, hoping to snap an 11-game losing streak. Unfortunately for Utah, the Spurs entered the game riding an 11-game winning streak of their own. Polar opposites. San Antonio pulled away in the final minutes, winning 110-102.

This is about as drastic of a matchup as you'll see in the NBA, but the Jazz came out hot, looking to build on the momentum they established against another one of the league's best teams, the Houston Rockets, who they narrowly lost to just a few days ago.

The Jazz put up 33 points in the first quarter, led by Mo Bamba, who scored 10. Speaking of Bamba, what an incredible performance he put together. While the Jazz ended up losing, this will forever be remembered as the Mo Bamba game.

Bamba finished with 26 points, five rebounds, four assists and three combined steals and blocks, highlighted by shooting a perfect 6-for-6 from 3-point range. The breakout game took a while for Bamba, but it finally happened.

The Jazz held a 10-point lead with just under two minutes remaining in the first quarter. The second quarter was a response from the Spurs, who eventually built a 10-point lead with nine minutes remaining in the third.

It looked as if the red-hot Spurs were going to run away with their 12th straight win.

Peterson went on to score eight straight points, making it look easy. He also could've easily earned a few trips to the free-throw line, yet he finished with zero attempts. As a team, the Jazz attempted just six free throws compared to San Antonio's 20.

It wasn't Peterson's best night, yet he still managed to demonstrate the talent that could lead him to receiving MVP votes someday. If a bad night for Peterson consists of 17 points, five rebounds, four assists and three combined steals and blocks, then goodness, everyone else is in trouble.

His efficiency was actually solid until the fourth quarter, when he simply couldn't get a shot to fall, going 0-for-5 in the final period. Several of his attempts came up short, leading me to wonder whether all the minutes Peterson has played are starting to wear him down just a little.

Peterson will be just fine, and he doesn't even turn 20 until January.

Keyonte George had another rough night, shooting under 30% from the field for the second time since returning from his ankle sprain. His shot selection was questionable at times, and that was the biggest difference between Peterson and George tonight. Neither was particularly efficient, but Peterson was generating good looks while George often found himself forcing difficult shots.

Isaiah Collier and Kyle Filipowski both received DNPs from head coach Will Hardy.

Josh Green and Josh Okogie both made positive contributions, with Green finishing at plus-4 and Okogie at plus-2. Svi Mykhailiuk, who has received plenty of criticism for his play, deserves some credit tonight after going 2-for-3 from beyond the arc and finishing with a team-high plus-15.

The Jazz are now a league-worst 1-13, having lost 12 consecutive games.

I know the injuries have been crazy. George missed the Miami game, and with a good performance from him in that matchup, Utah probably comes away with a win.

We also haven't seen projected starter Jusuf Nurkić yet, although he was going through some warmups before Sunday's game. Getting Nurkić back will help, but it won't solve everything. Don't expect him to shoot 6-for-6 from deep and score 26 points like Bamba did today.

Nobody can argue that missing two All-Star-caliber players isn't having a massive impact on this Jazz team right now. Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen are clearly missed.

That being said, there's still at least a month before Markkanen returns and probably a month and a half, minimum, before Jackson is back.

This current group has to figure something out. Otherwise, when the cavalry finally arrives, it might not matter.

And don't forget, Jaxson Hayes also missed today's game.

Will Hardy has to figure things out as soon as possible. At this point, it's not even about making the playoffs or the play-in tournament. It's about showing that he's capable of winning basketball games.

Right now, that's literally something the Jazz cannot do.

If one Dejounte Murray shot goes differently, the Jazz are sitting at 0-14.

I'm not sold on Hardy right now. These weird two-man games he runs, which seemingly always result in a contested jump shot during the final seconds of the shot clock, continue to infuriate and confuse me.

On the other side, Dylan Harper dominated the Jazz in the fourth quarter. Stephon Castle mostly had his way as well, using his strength to overpower Peterson on a few occasions.

Victor Wembanyama was mostly slowed down in the second half. After posting 21 points in the first half, he managed just five in the second. For a player of his stature, you'll take that.

The Jazz wasted an incredible performance from Bamba today. They played well enough to win, but for what feels like the hundredth time this season, Utah was unable to close out a game when it mattered most.

The young Jazz will search for answers Tuesday when they take on a Los Angeles Clippers team with just two wins of its own. Tipoff is scheduled for 9 p.m. MST.

#2651. ‘Best Commentary in the World,’ ‘Anyone Else Getting Sick?’ — NFL Fans Divided Over Tom Brady’s Spirited Reactions in 49ers-Cowboys Broadcast

Tom Brady had plenty to shout about during Sunday's game between the San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys. Whether viewers wanted to hear quite that much shouting became a separate contest.

His excited reactions had some fans laughing along and others wondering where they had left the remote.

San Francisco's 46-40 victory gave the FOX booth little opportunity to catch its breath. The 49ers scored three touchdowns covering at least 66 yards, turning routine-looking possessions into instant highlights. Brady's enthusiasm repeatedly spilled into the broadcast.

One particularly loud reaction accompanied Deebo Samuel's 70-yard touchdown on a third-quarter reverse. Samuel took a pitch from Kaelon Black and raced downfield, with Brock Purdy contributing as a blocker. Brady sounded thoroughly entertained as the play unfolded.

"TOM BRADY LEGIT LOST HIS MIND DURING THIS PLAY 😭,"one viewer wrote.

Another viewer happily boiled down Brady's contribution to one extended noise.

"Tom Brady with the best commentary in the world: 'OOOOOOOHHHHHHHHHH' 😭😭😭😭,"the fan wrote.

"The Tom Brady screams when he sees a big play are so hilarious 😭😭😭,"another fan added.

"Tom Brady put his soul into this scream [expletive] 😭😭😭,"one viewer joked.

There was certainly enough offense to justify some excitement. San Francisco sits second with aPFN Offense Impact Score of 88.9, and its ability to turn open space into touchdowns was on full display against Dallas.

For viewers enjoying Brady's reactions, those bursts of enthusiasm added another layer to the entertainment. A seven-time Super Bowl champion getting that worked up over a play can be pretty funny, especially when the analysis briefly gives way to a scream.

#2650. Cowboys' Brian Schottenheimer rips 'unacceptable' defense, 's***' tackling in loss to 49ers

Another week, another atrocious effort by the Dallas Cowboys' defense.

This time, it took place in a 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers that featured defensive backs Caleb Downs and Cobie Durant getting trucked on the same 25-yard touchdown run by backup rookie running back Kaelon Black.

It also featured 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy delivering downfield blocks on a 70-yard touchdown run in which Deebo Samuel Sr. went untouched.

It added up to a 29-point, 340-yard second half for the 49ers and a fundamental clinic by the Cowboys' defense on what not to do that could be featured on any high school teach tape.

The 49ers piled up 584 yards of offense on 9.4 yards per play. They rushed for 214 yards on 7.4 yards per carry. The 584 yards were the most allowed by the Cowboys in a home game in franchise history.

After the game, Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer didn't mince words when speaking with reporters about his defense. What choice did he have?

"I thought it was unacceptable," Schottenheimer said of the second-half defensive performance. "The tackling was atrocious. …

"At the end of the day, we tackled like s*** in the second half."

While pointed, Schottenheimer's comments didn't reveal anything that anybody who watched the game didn't already know. And it doesn't look like Dallas can fix this unit this year. At this point in a 4-6 Cowboys season, it appears as if nothing will.

In addition to Schottenheimer, critics have pointed to first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker as a potential target for change. But team owner Jerry Jones has stood by both this season, leaning on his lengthy track record of declining to make personnel changes before it's too late.

On Sunday, Jones maintained his support of Parker while pointing to his experience overseeing Super Bowl victories from more than 30 years ago to back up his reasoning.

"Again, it's what it is," Jones said postgame. "He's a young coach in his first year of coordinating and calling the plays. So you have to say that you would hope you could win games like the last that we've lost.

"I'll weigh his early times. I've been with teams that had some pretty good coordinators on defense that ended up winning Super Bowls."

Again, the last time a Cowboys team won the Super Bowl was after the 1995 season. This team is not going to end that streak. Thanks to an abysmal NFC East, though, the Cowboys remain reasonably in the playoff hunt, two games behind a not-great Giants team.

But there's little from the players on the field, the coaches on the sideline or the team owner in the luxury box that suggests the Cowboys have any hope of rallying to win the division.

#2649. Not a cold streak; the Utah Jazz are historically bad

When the buzzer sounded on San Antonio's 110-102 win in Salt Lake City, the reigning Western Conference champions tallied their 12th consecutive win, pushing their record to an NBA-leading 12-2. The Utah Jazz, losers of Sunday's Delta Center duel, likewise extended an active streak of 12 games. 12 losses in a row.

12 straight losses are tied for the second-longest losing streak in franchise history, but that's not even the worst part of this all.

This is only the second time the Jazz have started a season 1-13. The first time? The Jazz played their home games in New Orleans, Louisiana, and were playing their very first season as an NBA franchise. That 1974-75 team opened the season with a 1-16 record and fired head coach Scotty Robertson following their 14th loss.

This Utah Jazz team isn't just bad — they're historically bad.

Yes, this year's team has been playing at a deficit when it comes to injuries. They would have likely picked up a few more wins to this point were Jaren Jackson Jr., Jusuf Nurkic, and Lauri Markkanen not seated courtside, modeling the Polo Fall 2026 line at the end of the bench. Even so, Utah's foundation is riddled with cracks and is nowhere near the level of a playoff participant.

Undersized at the wing, Utah is consistently out-physicaled and outdone athletically against every team they've faced.

It's not all bad news, though. The Jazz's stars and veterans are all expected to return in a month or so, and they have already faced each of the Western Conference's top-six teams. After facing this slate in the early season, Utah's schedule will only get easier:

Even at full strength, Utah couldn't have reasonably expected to escape that gauntlet with a winning record.

The biggest issue facing the Jazz right now isn't injuries. It isn't inexperience. It isn't even personnel. The Jazz simply don't know how to win — they've never tried before.

It's a team that has grown accustomed to losing for the last four years, and those habits have reappeared night after night.

They took San Antonio and New Orleans into overtime, only to concede a 12-0 run in each of those additional five-minute periods. They fumbled away a 10-point third-quarter lead against Houston but clawed back to within one point at the 2:46 mark, only to relinquish a 2-8 run in crunch time. Down just one point against Memphis with one minute remaining, Utah failed to score again. Behind LA by one point with three minutes to go, the Jazz still couldn't seal the deal with JJJ and Markkanen active.

They've put themself in a position to win several times, but only once did they hold on to win.

How's this for glass-half-empty: Utah is one Dejounte Murray jumper away from being 0-14.

The Jazz front office continues to back Will Hardy as head coach, determined to support the man who patiently endured four years of non-competitive basketball to lead Utah back into the playoffs when the time is right. Just as Utah's roster is learning how to win in a competitive NBA, Hardy's baptism by fire has likewise left him a bit seared.

Now is not the time to take drastic measures — still 68 games to go in the season — but Utah's issues are buried much deeper than a string of bad luck.

Calvin Barrett is the Associate Editor for SLC Dunk and a Utah Jazz columnist for the Standard-Examiner. Originally from Springville, Utah, he currently writes from his desk in Japan.

#2646. Stats Rundown: 3 numbers to know from the Mavericks’ 131-94 loss at the Boston Celtics

The Dallas Mavericks lost in embarrassing fashion, 131-94 to the Boston Celtics Sunday night in Boston. This is the Mavericks third loss in a row to drop the team back to .500 at 7-7, with all three losses being fairly dispiriting.

It started awful and never got better, with the Mavericks trailing by a double-take-inducing 33 points at the end of the first quarter. The Mavericks had zero gumption or energy to start the game, after losing a game Saturday night to a Cleveland team with zero of their starters active.

Zaccharie Risacher led the Mavericks with 18 points. Jayson Tatum led Boston and all scorers with 32, as the Celtics shot over 50 percent from the field and over 40 percent from three.

It's early, but the Mavericks have reached their first crisis point of the season — if they want to be the surprise playoff team people thought after the team started 7-4, the turnaround has to happen quickly.

The Mavericks didn't shoot the ball poorly, considering their personnel, but even with 14 made threes, the Celtics still made nine more three pointers. It was a gap too wide to overcome.

Boston is a machine, and the Mavericks couldn't keep up. Dallas' defense features a lot of forwards and bigs, but the footspeed and defensive talent on the perimeter waxes and wanes — Dallas can recover with splashy defensive plays and deflections, but the team is prone to blow-bys since the Mavericks don't have much point-of-attack defense. The Celtics got the Mavericks into rotation early and Dallas never recovered.

After a meteroic start to the season, Flagg is officially in a slump. He was 5-of-15 against the Celtics, including 2-of-6 from three. Flagg has been under 40 percent from the field in four of the eight games he's played in November, and been under 45 percent in six of the eight. He's now shooting just 42 percent in November, and 26 percent from three.

Dallas' lineup did him no favors tonight, as Dusty May rolled out the Jason Kidd/Nico Harrison special from a year ago, with Flagg running point next to four non-shooting threats in PJ Washington, Caleb Martin, Naji Marshall, and Daniel Gafford. Washington and Martin have solid percentages this season, but they don't warp the defense with their spacing, especially without a lead guard to disrupt the defense. Flagg was seeing two, three, and even four bodies in front of him inside the three point line on just about every drive.

This is a problem for the Mavericks. Flagg is obviously a special talent, but the apex version of him is usually unlocked when next to a competent lead guard that can get downhill. We saw this last season and we've seen it again this season, as Dallas has played very well with Kyrie Irving and Flagg on the floor together. This is no knock on Flagg, but playing him without a credible guard talent next to him is like trying to win a game with one arm tied behind your back.

Unfortunately Dallas hasn't prioritized a lead guard in the last two offseasons. Dallas used the ninth overall pick in this summer's draft for Morez Johnson Jr., another big and then brought in another big in Santi Aldama via trade. Dallas' only guard moves were a smaller move for end-of-the-bench prospect Marcus Sasser, who's shown flashes, and using a late first-rounder for Sergio de Larrea, who is currently injured. Walter Clayton Jr. joined the team a week before the season started on a two-way contract and was almost immediately the team's backup point guard. The Dallas guard rotation is bleak, and especially so when guys like de Larrea and Max Christie are injured.

Bottom line: the Mavericks have to prioritize the guard position over the course of the next 18 months, whether that's at the upcoming trade deadline, next summer's draft, or the ensuing offseason. It's going to hold this whole thing back until it's resolved.

It says a lot about how bad Dallas is as a defensive rebounding team when the Celtics can get 18 offensive boards on a night where they were shooting the leather off the ball. There weren't a lot of misses for the Celtics to go get, and yet they still found themselves with a sizable offensive rebounding advantage (18-11).

Dallas cannot be this big of a team and still fail to rebound the ball consistently. It's just an untenable combination. If the Mavericks want to be a big, lengthy, athletic team, then they have to play like it. It does the team no good to be this big as a roster and this bad at rebounding. The trickle down effects are apparent. Nothing else to say, except the Mavericks just have to be better.
