The Roku Channel's new Christmas movie, Second Chance Holiday, premiered last Thursday, starring an actress in her first leading role: Ayesha Curry. The wife of Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry has 20 acting credits on IMDB, but has never headlined a movie before, and with that new stature has come criticism.

Arenas claimed that Curry speaks to other men via direct messages on social media because "she needs the attention because he doesn't give her the attention because he's focused," alluding to previous comments Curry made about having "zero male attention."

Former NFL running back LeSean McCoy also cited that conversation in criticizing Curry. "This is crazy. You got one of the greatest players of all time as your husband," McCoy said on Speakeasy. "I've seen a while ago where she keeps saying how she wants more attention, and how girls throw themselves at him and she still just wants to feel like she's wanted… now you want us to see kissing a dude?… This is crazy."

On Wednesday, Stephen Curry addressed the comments with a video on Instagram.

"Nick, Gil, Emmanuel and anybody else who feels the need to jump in and give an opinion on something you don't really know about, something that kind of speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do," Curry said. "Given the ignorance around how acting works, obviously I tried to laugh this one off but something needs to be said. Anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, kindly suggest that you just give the happy hands, the congratulations, and maybe the apology can be as loud as when y'all leading y'all shows with this topic."

Both Young, a former teammate of Curry's with the Warriors, and Arenas apologized Wednesday. "You my dog. I love you. If I said anything, I apologize like a man. I'm sorry," Young said.

"I'm sorry if he's offended; I didn't mean it like that. I was just saying, he's such a perfect dude," Arenas added, saying that Curry had never drawn controversy himself, but if someone in the family had, it was Ayesha.

NBA superstars are used to negativity from pundits, but commentary about their family is another matter. What Ayesha Curry does as an actress in a movie says nothing about her family or her husband's place in the basketball world. It's rare that Stephen Curry would address comments like this, but aside from the offense he and his family took, he was at least able to use it as a promotional opportunity.

"Appreciate the free pub, thank you for giving a nice shout-out to Second Chance Holiday," he said at the end of his video.

#2510. With Kirk Cousins back, the Vikings really can win the Super Bowl and here's how

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Three weeks ago, the Minnesota Vikings were 6-0, a remarkable achievement given their offense was among the worst in the NFL. Brian Flores' defense was playing at a historically dominant level, and the question wasn't whether they could win games this way – it was whether they could keep doing it all the way to the Super Bowl.

I know, that seems like a silly thing to write – forget about even saying it out loud – but there's precedent!

But since winning six straight to start the season, the Vikings have lost two in a row, the offense has somehow gotten worse, and following one of the most historically inept quarterback performances in 35 years, the team traded a third-round pick for 38-year-old Kirk Cousins.

According to TruMedia, NFL QBs have attempted at least 25 passes in a game 14,463 times since 1990.Carson Wentz's performance on MNF vs. the Bills ranks:• 15th-worst passer rating (8.9)• T-27th-worst completion rate (32%)• 12th-worst EPA/dropback (-0.85, since 2000)

A year ago, such a move would've seemed supremely desperate because Cousins was still in Atlanta sharing time with Michael Penix Jr., the quarterback the Falcons drafted not long after signing Cousins to a huge deal in 2024.  And during those two seasons, Cousins barely resembled the version we had seen in Minnesota, the one who made Justin Jefferson look like he actually enjoyed playing football. (I suppose it didn't hurt that Jefferson averaged 98 receiving yards per game when Cousins was the Vikings QB throwing the passes.)

Now, that very same trade just seems … moderately desperate, and that has everything to do with the trifecta of ineffectiveness that was JJ McCarthy, Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz. And after Cousins helped the Vikings get back in the win column Sunday against Green Bay – at the same stadium where he tore his Achilles in his final game with Minnesota three years ago – that Super Bowl question suddenly sounds much less ridiculous.

Because here's the thing: The Vikings don't need Cousins to play like an MVP. They don't even need him to lead a top-10 offense. Hell, above average – even average – could be good enough. History is full of teams that won championships with replacement-level offenses and dominant defenses, and Minnesota is unequivocally closer to joining that group than they were a week ago.

When we first wrote about the Vikings' Super Bowl chances in late October, they ranked 31st in offensive efficiency, averaging just 18.8 points per game despite that 6-0 start.

Two games later … they're still 31st in offensive efficiency, and their scoring average has somehow fallen (it was 18.3 coming into Week 10). Meanwhile, Flores' defense continues to carry this team. They're allowing just 14.5 points per game, and opponents have struggled to move the ball consistently against a defense that blitzes on 74% of dropbacks, more than twice the league average (32.8%) and easily the highest rate in the NFL.

That formula has been good enough for six wins in eight games. But there's a difference between surviving the regular season and winning three or four consecutive playoff games against the NFC's best teams.

In his first game back with the Vikings, Cousins led the team to 30 points Sunday. The last time this group scored 30? Week 1 … against these very same Packers. This time around, Cousins tossed two touchdowns (good luck finding someone – anyone – happier than Justin Jefferson, who finished with 9 catches for 74 yards).

COUSINS TO MYLES PRICE FOR A TD ON 3RD AND 23MINvsGB on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jSQvCluTla

Kirk Cousins to Gavin Bartholomew for the TD pic.twitter.com/g1YUgVp8nr

But the defense was even more impressive, sacking Jordan Love eight times — the most by any team in a game this season — and forcing three turnovers.

Cousins looked like a shell of himself during his time in Atlanta, which ain't unreasonable for a quarterback in his mid-30s coming off Achilles surgery. That said, he had manifested 2023 Pre-Injury Kirk this season for the Raiders. Through nine games, he'd thrown 20 touchdown passes against eight interceptions, with a 97.1 passer rating.

More importantly, he's been substantially more efficient than the QBs Minnesota had trotted out through the first two months (admittedly, it would be hard to be less efficient). So, how much of a difference could that make over the next 2-3 months?

Based on how Cousins has played this season compared to Murray and Wentz, Minnesota's offense could go from averaging just 18.3 points per game to as many as 27 when you look at expected points added per dropback (which is just a measure of how much a quarterback helps or hurts his team's chances of scoring). That's the best-case scenario, but even a more modest improvement could mean the Vikings score 4-6 more points per game.

And we don't even have to assume Cousins will replicate everything he's done in Las Vegas. Here's what Minnesota's offense could look like if he's something less than that.

How much better could the Vikings offense be with Cousins?

Projections use Cousins' 2026 passing efficiency compared with Minnesota's previous quarterbacks.

The "solid improvement" projection puts Minnesota at 25 points per game, nearly seven more than it's averaging now. Even "modest improvement" gets the Vikings to 22.7, which might not sound all that impressive until you consider what some previous Super Bowl champions managed offensively.

And there's another obvious reason this could work and it doesn't require advanced stats, just eyes and common sense: Cousins has already shown he can run Kevin O'Connell's offense at a high level. In 2022, he threw for 4,547 yards and 29 touchdowns and Minnesota finished 13-4. He was playing well again the following season before tearing his Achilles. Now, some three years later, time is a flat circle.

Look, it's easy to win a Super Bowl with a Hall of Fame quarterback – at least easier than winning one with a replacement-level passer leading an average offense. There's a reason Patrick Mahomes, Tom Brady and Peyton Manning have a combined 12 rings.

But there is more than one way to crack an egg. (I reflexively wrote 'to skin a cat,' but then spent 15 minutes figuring out whether people still say that, and if it's even acceptable. I went with the egg idiom instead. Getting old is weird.) And for the Vikings, that means a lights-out defense and something approaching an average offense.

Luckily, history has plenty of such success stories that ended in hoisting the Lombardi Trophy.

Super Bowl champions that won without dominant offenses

Five of the Super Bowl champs averaged between 20.8 and 22.2 points per game. Even if we go with "modest improvement" for the Vikings and Cousins, it would put them above all five.

So what lessons does history give us about how Minnesota could win the whole thing?

Baltimore might be the most famous example of a defense carrying an offense to a title. Ray Lewis and company allowed just 10.3 points per game, the fewest ever in a 16-game season, while their offense went five consecutive games without scoring a touchdown. Five! The Ravens eventually replaced Tony Banks with Trent Dilfer, who was a game manager in the best sense of the phrase. Baltimore finished 12-4 and won Super Bowl XXXV, beating the Giants 34-7. Minnesota's defense isn't quite at that level, but Cousins is a considerable upgrade over Dilfer.

Tampa Bay's defense, led by Derrick Brooks, Warren Sapp, John Lynch and Ronde Barber, allowed just 12.3 points per game. Brad Johnson threw 22 touchdowns and only six interceptions during the regular season, but the Bucs still ranked 18th in scoring. They didn't need an explosive passing game because their defense consistently put them in position to win. In the Gruden (Super) Bowl, Tampa Bay intercepted Raiders quarterback Rich Gannon five times, including three(!) pick-sixes, and they cruised to a 48-21 win. Again, Cousins is an upgrade over Johnson, but the lesson remains: Take care of the football, make the throws that are there, and let the defense do the rest.

Pittsburgh allowed just 13.9 points per game behind James Harrison, Troy Polamalu, LaMarr Woodley and Bryant McFadden, but its offense – specifically the offensive line – was on the struggle bus all season. Ben Roethlisberger was sacked 46 times, the running game was inconsistent, and the Steelers averaged just 21.7 points per game. Yet when Pittsburgh needed a touchdown in Super Bowl XLIII, Roethlisberger delivered, leading a 78-yard drive capped by that catch by Santonio Holmes in the back corner of the end zone. The Steelers beat Arizona 27-23. And that's where Cousins could make the biggest difference for Minnesota over Murray or Wentz: Flores' defense can keep games close, but someone still has to win them.

This was the comp that got my attention a few weeks ago, when the Vikings started 6-0 with no real offense to speak of. Manning was 39, his arm strength had diminished following four neck surgeries earlier in his career, and he threw nine touchdowns against 17 interceptions in only 10 games. Brock Osweiler started seven games, and Denver finished 25th in offensive efficiency. None of that stopped Von Miller, DeMarcus Ware and the Broncos defense from carrying Denver through Pittsburgh, New England and Carolina to win Super Bowl 50. The Vikings' current offense has somehow been worse, but Cousins will close that gap considerably. And unlike Manning in 2015, Cousins has been playing some of his best football this season.

Kansas City won its second consecutive Super Bowl despite an offense that barely looked like the explosive units we'd become accustomed to watching. The Chiefs averaged 21.8 points per game, their receivers struggled with drops, and the offense committed way too many turnovers. Mahomes remained Mahomes, of course, but Steve Spagnuolo's defense allowed just 17.3 points per game and gave Kansas City a chance to win those games when it couldn't just outscore the opponent. In the Super Bowl, Mahomes orchestrated the winning touchdown drive against the 49ers in overtime. Cousins will never be confused for Mahomes, but the larger point remains: Even great QBs sometimes need a defense capable of carrying them into the postseason.

Seattle won last season's Super Bowl with Sam Darnold under center and Mike Macdonald overseeing one of the NFL's best defenses. The Seahawks averaged 28.4 points per game, considerably more than the other champions above, but they also committed 28 turnovers (second-most in the NFL) and ranked just 11th in points per offensive drive. In the Super Bowl, Darnold threw for 202 yards and one touchdown, while Kenneth Walker III rushed for 135 yards. Meanwhile, the defense sacked Drake Maye six times, forced four turnovers and held New England scoreless through three quarters in a 29-13 win. Minnesota doesn't need Cousins to put up 30 points every week, either. It needs him to protect the football, sustain drives and give that defense a chance to win games without having to carry the offense for four quarters.

There's no guarantee Minnesota's defense will remain this dominant, either. Through eight games, the Vikings have played at a level matched by only 14 other defenses (out of 481!) over the past 15 seasons. But history suggests that's difficult to sustain. Among the 17 teams that started at a similar level, 13 continued to play above-average defense, but most weren't nearly as dominant the rest of the way.

The 2019 Patriots D is a good example. They were almost impossibly good through eight games, but their performance fell off considerably over the second half of the season. New England finished 12-4 and lost its first playoff game.

The good news? Minnesota might not need Flores' defense to maintain that pace if Cousins can get the offense moving. Asking the defense to carry a bottom-five offense through the NFC playoffs is one thing. Asking it to support a team averaging 23 or 25 points per game is something else entirely.

Minnesota already won six games with an offense that ranked among the NFL's worst. Cousins helped make it seven Sunday with a 20-point win over their division rivals.

Flores has built a defense capable of shutting down good teams, and the Vikings have spent the first half of the season proving they can win with little help from whoever the quarterback is.

But winning in January and February is another matter. The Vikings don't need Cousins to be Mahomes or Brady or vintage Peyton. They need him to make the throws – many of them routine – that Minnesota's other quarterbacks haven't or couldn't, protect the football, and give their all-galaxy defense some margin for error. History has made it very clear that can be enough to win a Super Bowl.

FanDuel SGP price: +101  (subject to change)

The relationship between the Jets and their best-ever player in Hellebuyck, who was also the primary goalie for gold medal-winning Team USA in the Winter Olympics, had been strained for a while. Then it broke over the summer when he publicly demanded a trade and stayed away from the club until he got it. Hellebuyck is in the third year of a seven-year contract extension with an $8.5 million average annual value and said it was about family and not money.

The 2024-25 Hart Trophy winner preferred Florida, but the sides couldn't agree on that deal. On Oct. 23 the Jets sent him to New Jersey for Dawson Mercer, Alexander Command, Nick Bjugstad, goalie Nico Daws, a 2029 second-round pick and a 2027 seventh-round pick. That date was important, as it was the day Hellebuyck's suspension by Winnipeg was set to end and he was expected to report. He waived his no-movement clause to facilitate the trade.

Things might have gotten ugly without a deal, but Hellebuyck became simply the latest prominent American NHL player to push for a move from a Canadian club, following the likes of Brady Tkachuk and Quinn Hughes.

Hellebuyck is reviled now in Winnipeg, so it's a massive shame the Devils will let him rest tonight, and boy is the team getting ripped for the decision – it almost makes this a bigger deal now. It certainly wasn't Hellebuyck's decision to sit, as GM Sunny Mehta announced the following after Hellebuyck pitched a shutout Sunday in Toronto.

"Connor Hellebuyck was adamant that he felt a duty to play on Tuesday in Winnipeg," Mehta wrote in a statement. "However, in our estimation, playing in this game would potentially give us a reduction in our expected win probability."

Bet on the NHL and more at FanDuel, where bettors can get up to $200 in bonus bets:

Hellebuyck said he is "disappointed … but when you're looking at what's best for the team, I understand where they're coming from." Sitting a future Hall of Famer and Olympic gold medalist in his prime who is 5-0-0 with a 1.96 goals-against average and a .913 save percentage since joining the Devils lowers your team's expected win probability? Yeah, OK.

This likely was because of the bitter reactions Tkachuk got in Ottawa and Hughes did in Vancouver in their returns this season. #2506. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.

#2505. LOOK: Fernando Mendoza scores first NFL TD on opening drive vs. Seahawks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With Kirk Cousins traded back to the Minnesota Vikings, Las Vegas Raiders fans' wait to see 2026 first-round pick Fernando Mendoza start is over. Some waited to jump for joy upon Mendoza scoring a touchdown at home against the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks in Week 10 until he scores his second touchdown.

The time to celebrate didn't take long. Mendoza capped Las Vegas' 11-play, 46-yard opening drive with a 10-yard touchdown run reminisicent of his national championship scoring scramble against the Miami Hurricanes in January.

Fernando Mendoza rushes it in for his first career TD 🗣️SEAvsLV on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/gcKUNMIZUH

The reason behind this is a wholesome one. Mendoza's mother, Elsa, utilizes a wheelchair while dealing with multiple sclerosis (MS), so fans are trying to organize a tribute to her, Mendoza, and his family by remaining seated if/when he scores against Seattle on Sunday. For those who watched Mendoza's college career, TV cameras often cut to his family celebrating, and Mendoza's father, Fernando Sr., would often be seen seated and hugging Elsa after touchdowns. Fernando Sr. also remained seated as he and Elsa's son was drafted first overall in the 2026 NFL draft.

"I see her fighting every single day, and with a smile on her face," Mendoza said of his mother during a pre-draft appearance on The Rich Eisen Show. "So there's no excuse for me to have a bad day, bad play or bad game. I'm always trying to have an optimistic approach, give the best and serve the best to my teammates."

Obviously, there will still be Raiders fans who got so excited that they left their seats when Mendoza scored his first NFL touchdown, but it's a thoughtful gesture.

Listen, everyone going to Allegiant Stadium this Sunday. Stay seated when Fernando scores his first touchdown. Will be an epic gesture from fans to player. Pass it along.

Mendoza is the first No. 1 overall quarterback in NFL history to make his first career start versus the defending Super Bowl champions. Seattle also entered Week 10 leading the entire league in total defense (244.2 total yards per game allowed), which means Mendoza will also be the first No. 1 overall pick quarterback to make his first career start against the NFL's No. 1 total defense since Vinny Testaverde in 1987. However, new Raiders coach Klint Kubiak was the Seahawks offensive coordinator last season, so perhaps he told Mendoza some vulnerabilities the Seahawks defense has that other teams may not be as aware of.

Either way, many Raiders fans are glued to their seats at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday afternoon.

#2502. MLB rumors: Phillies OF on the trading block, Blue Jays eye ex-Yankee, plus Mets, Mariners, Braves, Rays, more

Thursday marks the final day of the General Manager meetings in Las Vegas. Though we haven't seen any major moves this offseason, we have seen an uptick in rumors in the past few days and that isn't a coincidence. Put a bunch of reporters and front-office execs in the same area for three or four days and chatter picks up, even if there isn't a ton of actual substance behind it.

Rumors are always fun, so let's round up the latest right here in addition to any news.

We have one of our first major-league deals of the offseason as the Braves have signed reliever Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million deal. Phillips ranked No. 34 on our top 50 free agent list.

Phillips, a 32-year-old right-hander, has been a setup man or closer for the Dodgers for the last several seasons. In returning from surgery last season, he appeared in 31 games, pitching to a 3.46 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 33 strikeouts in 26 innings. The majority of his closing experience came in 2023 when he had 24 saves in 27 chances.

The Braves' closer last season was Raisel Iglesias, but he's a free agent. Holdover Robert Suarez could take over those duties while Phillips, lefty Dylan Lee and youngster Didier Fuentes are also in the late-inning mix.

The Blue Jays went from one of the best offensive teams in 2025 to one of the worst in 2026. They'd love a big bounceback from Vladimir Guerrero Jr., among other positive movements, but they also look for outside help. Might that help come in the form of free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr.?

The Jays have met with representatives for Chisholm, reports Sportsnet.

Chisholm, 28, hit .231/.312/.399 last season, but had a huge 2025 and any signing team would be hoping for the 2025 version of Chisholm.

The Jays do have a capable incumbent second baseman in Ernie Clement, but either Clement or Chisholm can be used in the outfield and the Blue Jays certainly need outfield upgrades.

The Phillies have been telling opposing teams that they are not "locked into anything" regarding their current outfield situation, according to The Athletic, so much so that All-Star outfielder Brandon Marsh is available in a trade.

As things stand, with Bryce Harper moving back to first base, the Phillies would have Bryan De La Cruz in right, Justin Crawford in center and Marsh in left, but that all seems pretty fluid as they look to upgrade the ballclub and keep that window of contention open.

Marsh, 28, had a stellar start last season, leading to his first-ever All-Star Game. Through July 1, he hit .319/.352/.530. The rest of the way, however, he slashed .177/.241/.241, dragging him down overall to a 90 OPS+ and 0.4 WAR on the season.

The Mariners have shown interest in free agent left fielder Ian Happ, per MLB Network.

Happ, 32, has spent his entire 10-year MLB career with the Cubs, who drafted him in the first round all the way back in 2015. He was pretty consistent from 2022-25, averaging 3.9 WAR with a .251/.347/.433 (118 OPS+) line and winning four Gold Gloves. Last season, though, he dipped to .218/.326/.412 (103 OPS+) with 2.7 WAR. He still topped 20 home runs for the fifth time in the last six years.

The Mariners have a vacancy in left field with Randy Arozarena having hit free agency and a need to upgrade their offense.

Yesterday's big news was the Yankees' interest in free agent first/third baseman Alec Bohm and The Athletic reports that we can now add the Mets to the list of suitors.

Bohm hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with 15 home runs, 88 RBI and -0.2 WAR last season. It might be surprising to see him garnering such interest on the open market, but there isn't much right-handed power out there and Bohm finished last season strong (.318/.402/.453 in his last 42 games). The Mets, meanwhile, are desperate for help at the cold corner after last year's disastrous Jorge Polanco experiment. Jared Young did provide a glimmer of hope at first base before suffering a concussion in September while colliding with a teammate on a play.

Free agent starting pitcher Dustin May has a decent market right now, according to MLB Network, with at least the Cubs, White Sox, Padres and Astros having shown interest in the right-hander.

May, 29, made 31 starts between the Cardinals and Brewers last season, going 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA in 145 ⅔ innings. He showed flashes of brilliance with the Cardinals and had a stretch from April 10 to June 15 during which he posted a 2.54 ERA in 12 starts, but in the end there was plenty of inconsistency and even bad, forcing him into a bullpen role in the playoffs for the champion Brewers.

Free agent catcher Ryan Jeffers has been extended the qualifying offer from the Twins, meaning he has to decide by net Tuesday whether to accept the one-year, $23.15 million contract or hit free agency. There's nothing that says a team can't re-sign a player after he declines their qualifying offer, of course, and it sounds like that path is possible in this case.

Jeffers will decline the QO and the Twins are interested in reaching a multi-year deal to bring him back, reports the Minnesota Star-Tribune. Jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs for Minnesota in 2026, a standout line for a catcher, though he missed several months with a broken hamate. The Twins do have several catchers in their farm system, including Vahn Lackey, the No. 3 pick in last year's draft, and Eduardo Tait, who headlined the trade return for Jhoan Duran.

Much has been said and will continue to be said about the 2027 free agent class and how it looks relatively weak, especially on the position-player side, where the best players are the likes of Jazz Chisholm Jr., Seiya Suzuki, and the aforementioned Arozarena and Jeffers.

As we know, the Rays love to find avenues where they can exploit market inefficiencies. Their latest move might be to hit the trade market with center fielder Jonny DeLuca in anticipation of moving Victor Mesa Jr. to center, according to The Athletic.

DeLuca, 28, got more playing time than ever before in 2026, appearing in 112 games and getting 370 plate appearances. He hit .266/.300/.429 (101 OPS+) with 11 homers, 50 RBI, 17 steals and 1.7 WAR.

Fresh off a playoff berth despite the lowest payroll in all of baseball at a paltry $75ish million, the Guardians are planning to increase payroll. Or so they say.

"We'll go up," club president Chris Antonetti told The Athletic. "We have to."

The Guardians hosted six playoff games and made some money there, not to mention that they have a bunch of players hitting arbitration and surely they want to spend more to remain competitive. There's an added wrinkle here, too, which would be that the ownership side is really pushing hard for a salary cap when the upcoming CBA expires in a few weeks. With a cap comes a floor and we've seen MLB float proposals with salary floors in the $180 million range, or well more than double what the Guardians had last season.

So, yeah, I'd say the Guardians "have to" increase payroll, one way or another.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez has won the 2026 American League MVP, the BBWAA announced Thursday night.

The Baseball Writers' Association of America ballot uses two voters from each of the 15 chapters housing AL teams. Each voter submits a ballot with 10 players, ranked 1-10. A first-place vote gets a player 14 points, while second place earns nine, third place eight, etc., until a 10th-place vote earns one point. Ballots are due before the playoffs begin, as this is a regular-season award.

Alvarez, 29, bounced back from an injury-riddled disaster in 2025, during which he only played in 48 games. This time around, he avoided the IL and appeared in 158 games. He hit .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+) with 34 doubles, a triple, 42 home runs, 106 RBI, 105 runs and 6.8 WAR. He made a late run at the Triple Crown, missing out by one home run and seven RBI. He did lead the majors in all three triple slash categories, though, leading in average by five points, on-base percentage by a whopping 42 points -- he led the majors in walks -- and 31 points in slugging percentage. Add the latter two and his OPS victory was 90 points -- 1.033 to second place's .943 (National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong).

The only players in MLB history to lead the majors in all three triple slash categories:

Alvarez becomes just the third Astros player to win MVP after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017.

Rays third baseman Junior Caminero finished in second. At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. came in third. This is now his fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

#2496. Chiefs trade deadline move for Josh Downs unlocks MVP Patrick Mahomes of old

Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs' deep-strike passing game appeared dead and gone through nine weeks of the 2026 season.

However, Chiefs general manager Brett Veach's NFL trade deadline acquisition of Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs Tuesday afternoon brought the two-time NFL MVP version of Mahomes and the team's downfield passing attack back to life in Week 10.

Entering Week 9, Mahomes was averaging an NFL-worst 5.6 air yards per pass attempt and had become the only quarterback in the last 20 years to average under 5.0 air yards per pass attempt in four consecutive games in the same season, per Pro Football Focus. That four-game dry spell coincided with the ankle dislocation for deep threat wide receiver Tyquan Thornton in Week 4. A week ago, Mahomes was grabbing his right elbow in pain after the New York Jets bent it backward, and on Sunday, the Patrick Mahomes of old returned.

The introduction of Downs and his ability to threaten defenses out of the slot and down the field changed everything. Downs' 1,995 receiving yards out of the slot were the second-most in the NFL in his career since he entered the league in 2023 at the start of Week 10, trailing only Detroit Lions All-Pro wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (2,160).

Mahomes, as a result, marched into Atlanta like Union General William T. Sherman in 1864 and burned the Falcons' secondary to the ground at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, completing 22 of 35 passes for 348 yards, 5 passing touchdowns, and no interceptions in a 35-13 win for the visiting Chiefs. Sunday marked Mahomes' first game with at least five passing touchdowns since the opening week of the 2022 NFL season, the year of his second and most recent league MVP season. He averaged 9.3 air yards per pass attempt, his most since Week 4 at the Las Vegas Raiders, the game Thornton went down.

Mahomes had not one but two touchdown passes of 20-plus air yards, which snapped a 20-game drought without a passing touchdown of 20-plus air yards. That was the second-longest such streak of his career. Downs' arrival coincided with a number of different droughts ending for the three-time Super Bowl MVP on Sunday.

It was clear Mahomes was throwing with a different level of confidence with Downs on the field. He rifled a dart of a back-shoulder touchdown to Downs from 18 yards out, and that set the tone for the rest of the afternoon. He finished with 4 catches on 5 targets for 53 yards, including that 18-yard receiving touchdown. The box score doesn't fully capture the gravity he brought to the Chiefs' passing game, which is more apparent on some of Mahomes' other highlight throws from Sunday's demolition in Atlanta.

"It [was] good to see guys step up and make plays, especially against man coverage," Mahomes said in an understatement postgame, via Fox 4 News Kansas City.

Mahomes steps up and drops a dime to Josh Downs for a TD!KCvsATL on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dwTMy1qZYC

His next touchdown toss was a 39-yard effortless throw to fifth-round rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen, and the Falcons had no safety help on the play.

3rd touchdown pass for Mahomes! Cyrus Allen scores on a 39-yarder.KCvsATL on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Nijm7zG3lT

That was just a warm-up for Mahomes' 50-yard rocket launch of a pass down the middle of the field to wide receiver Rashee Rice, his longest pass of the day.

Mahomes & Rice connect deep for 50 yards!KCvsATL on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ZFDULxVq7n

His final touchdown throw of the day came on a classic Mahomes roll out into a deep strike score from 43 yards out to undrafted wide receiver Andrew Armstrong.

348 yards & 5 TDs for @PatrickMahomes 👏 pic.twitter.com/WUMyRQsznx

The rest of the AFC, and the NFL at large, for that matter, are now on notice because the arrival of Downs awakened MVP Mahomes once again.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Things got heated between the Rockets and Warriors on Wednesday, with Marcus Smart getting ejected late in the third quarter for throwing a punch at the head area of Golden State's Charles Bassey.

Smart and Bassey had gotten tangled up on the other end. After they disconnected and Bassey made his way back on defense, Smart chased after Bassey from behind, made contact, swung around to his front side, and threw the blow that is likely going to lead to a suspension.

MARCUS SMART PUNCHES CHARLES BASSEY 😳 pic.twitter.com/MUsLlDHCz4

What did Bassey do, or say, that got Smart so riled up?

"I just talked to [Smart]. He said they got wrapped up, and [Smart]'s elbow that he hurt got bent up," Rockets coach Ime Udoka explained after the game. "So, [Smart] said something to him. Bassey said, 'What are you going to do?' And he did it."

You can see a better view of the play here.

Looks Like Charles Bassey Had His Arm Tangled Up With Marcus Smart Before The Punch.Nothing Too Serious, Why Did He React Like That? https://t.co/d96UmqUDpM pic.twitter.com/5tmUbokqHR

Smart was hit with a flagrant-2 foul, which carries an automatic ejection (the 13th of Smart's career). Smart didn't stick around long after he threw the punch. As players were being separated to keep things from escalating any further, Smart almost immediately took off his elbow sleeve and walked straight to the locker room. He knew he was gone.

As for Bassey's side of the story, the Warriors' big man said Smart was "playing dirty" all night.

"He's been playing dirty the whole game," Bassey said. "In the first half, I was trying to set a screen and he grabbed my knee. So I mean, he was playing dirty. [On the play in question], I think I was trying to get a rebound and he was grabbing my hand and I was trying to run back on defense. ... And then he got up on me and swung. Obviously that was weak. I think that was, honestly, fake toughness."

Asked whether he said anything to Smart to set him off, Bassey explained: "He said something to me. He said something like, 'Hey, don't do that.' I said, 'Do what?' It's a grown-man's league."

Charles Bassey calls out Marcus Smart for being a fake tough guy and a dirty player 😬(Via @anthonyVslater ) pic.twitter.com/l461taMhtS

As for how long Smart will be out, here's the league's wording on punches thrown from the NBA's official rule book.

So Smart is out at least one game and, again, almost certainly a good chunk of cash.
